subject: head rush
title: What If You Stood Up Too Fast?

scenes.text: What if you stood up too fast? For a moment, your brain runs short of blood.
The instant you rise, gravity drags roughly half a litre to a litre of blood into your legs and trunk.
Within seconds, less blood returns to your heart and pressure dips. Vision blurs and your head goes light.
Pressure sensors in your neck catch the drop. Your heart speeds up by about 10 to 15 beats a minute.
Your veins tighten and push blood back up. In most people, the fix is quick and nobody notices.
You do this every morning. A head rush is just the day your reflex is a beat too slow.

description:
What if you stood up too fast? Standing normally pools roughly 0.5 to 1 litre of blood in the leg and trunk veins, briefly lowering blood pressure, according to the Merck Manual.
Pressure sensors in the aorta and carotid arteries react by speeding the heart (typically 10-15 beats a minute) and tightening vessels; when that reflex lags, you get a head rush.
